paragraphs: Rabbana Nechemiah and his brother Mar Ukva, sons of Rav's daughter.
In Chullin 92a they said of them that they are among the proud princes [or: great leaders] of Israel.
And they were students of Rav Chisda, as in Bava Batra 51b, where they said to Rav Chisda, "Does the master abandon the great ones (Rav) and act in accord with the small one (Rabbi Elazar)?"

And in Shabbat 20b: Ravin and Abaye were sitting before Rabbana Nechemiah, brother of the Resh Galuta; they saw him wearing silk, and from this it is implied that his brother Mar Ukva was the Resh Galuta. But the reading of Dikdukei Soferim is: Rabbana Nechemiah the Resh Galuta. And we find in Bava Metzia 91b: Rav Ashi said, "This matter was asked of me by the household of Rav Nechemiah the Resh Galuta [Hyman proposes Rabbana in place of Rav, following Dikdukei Soferim and Maharshal]," etc. And it is a great wonder: was not the Resh Galuta in the time of Rav Ashi Huna bar Natan? And I found a precious reading in Dikdukei Soferim from manuscript siglum ה׳ that was written "Rabbana the Resh Galuta," and from this was made "Rav Nechemiah the Resh Galuta."

notes.text: The readings disagree about whether Nechemya or his brother was the exilarch. Hyman questions the Rav Ashi chronology and cites a manuscript reading Rabbana without Nechemya; ה׳ is its manuscript siglum.

Chullin 92a directly applies the proud-princes description to Ukva and Nechemya, sons of Rav’s daughter. Hyman’s competing exilarch readings, Rav Ashi chronological objection and reconstruction from manuscript siglum ה׳ remain his argument; the exact Dikdukei Soferim and Maharshal printings were not inspected.
